subject: physics
title: Momentum
summary: Momentum is the 'motion of mass' — how much 'get-up-and-go' a moving object carries, computed as mass × velocity. A loaded truck creeping along and a baseball hurtling in both have momentum. Explore how momentum builds, transfers in collisions, and is always conserved.

crossReferences.label: Mass (Mechanics)
crossReferences.note: Momentum = mass × velocity, so mass is one of the two knobs that set the momentum.

crossReferences.label: Velocity (Mechanics)
crossReferences.note: Velocity is the other momentum knob — and it supplies the direction, making momentum a vector.

crossReferences.label: Force (Mechanics)
crossReferences.note: A force applied for a time (impulse) is what changes momentum — Newton's second law in momentum form.

compareCandidate.label: Momentum vs. force
compareCandidate.description: A force is a push or pull applied now; momentum is the motion an object already has from its mass and velocity. Forces transfer momentum between objects.

plainLanguageExplanation: Momentum is the amount of 'motion' bottled in a moving object — the quantity that makes a fast bowling ball hard to stop and a slow truck even harder. The formula is simple: momentum = mass × velocity. Double the mass or double the velocity and you double the momentum. Because velocity has a direction, momentum does too — a ball going left has momentum pointing left. The superpower of momentum is that it cannot be created or destroyed: when two carts collide, the momentum lost by one is gained by the other, so the total before equals the total after. That's conservation of momentum — the reason a cannon recoils when you fire it and why a skater glides forward after throwing a backpack backward. In the model, two carts on a track roll into each other: set their masses and speeds, press Go, and watch them exchange velocity arrows while the total-momentum banner never changes.

whyItMatters: Momentum is the concept behind collisions of every scale — car safety design (crumple zones extend crash time), sports (why follow-through matters), and rocketry (how a rocket moves by throwing gas backward). It explains why heavier moving objects are harder to stop and why momentum can never just vanish; it's a threshold that makes the whole 'collision' part of physics predictable. Understanding momentum is the launch pad for impulse and, later, energy.
didYouKnow: A rocket in space doesn't overcome a wall of air — it throws a little gas backward. That is momentum conservation at work: the engine pushes gas one way, and the ship pushes itself the other way onto a new course.
compareReason: A push or pull (force) versus the motion already possessed (momentum) — bumping two carts shows exactly how one gets transferred without ever being destroyed.
